title: CompUSA (1984–2008): post-mortem · Spectre Brands
description: How the first chain of computer superstores grew to $6.3 billion in sales, was bought by Carlos Slim for $10.10 a share and closed its last 103 stores, traced through its filings, with charts, commercials and archived pages.

card.blurb: The first chain of computer superstores sold $6.3 billion of PCs a year at its height. Then the PC turned into a cheap commodity that Best Buy, Dell and everyone else sold too.

stat.label: stores left to close in December 2007

hero.dates: Founded in Dallas in 1984 as Soft Warehouse. Sold to a restructuring firm on Dec 7, 2007, which closed the stores. Brand retired by its last owner in 2012.
hero.standfirst: It taught America to buy a computer the way it bought a refrigerator. Then America learned to buy one anywhere.
hero.deck: CompUSA opened the first computer superstore in 1988 and had 211 of them eleven years later, selling $6.3 billion of hardware, software and training a year. Its own annual report explained the problem: customers needed less help and cared more about price. Carlos Slim’s companies took it private in 2000 for $10.10 a share and spent seven years trying to turn it around. The page draws on CompUSA’s SEC filings, the filings of its owners and buyers, contemporary press and the archived website. The company was private for its last eight years, so the record is thinner there, and the page says so.

findings.title: It started level with Best Buy.
findings.text: In fiscal 1992 CompUSA sold $823M and Best Buy $930M. By fiscal 1999 it was $6.3B against $10.1B, and Best Buy sold computers as one of four product categories.[^1][^2][^23]

findings.title: The stores sold less every year after 1996.
findings.text: Sales per square foot fell from $1,405 in fiscal 1996 to $1,139 in fiscal 1999. The company blamed lower selling prices for desktops, notebooks and monitors.[^2]

findings.title: The best year earned two cents on the dollar.
findings.text: Net income peaked at $93.9M in fiscal 1997, or 2.0% of $4.61B in sales. Two years later the company lost $45.7M.[^2]

findings.title: Buying the rival did not help.
findings.text: CompUSA paid about $175M for Computer City in 1998 and closed 59 of its 96 U.S. stores. The ones it kept sold $711 a square foot against $1,177 at its own.[^2]

findings.title: A rich owner bought seven more years.
findings.text: Carlos Slim’s companies took CompUSA private in 2000. In February 2007 it closed 126 stores; in December it sold what was left to a firm that closed it.[^5][^12][^13]
